beatText.opening.assembly: 01 / THE QUESTION Between code and the bench. How do you connect a firmware decision to something you can actually observe? I wrote the firmware, scheduled the power states and built the bring-up fixture for Mosslink, an environmental sensor. Firmware is code that controls a physical device. ↓ Follow the work
beatText.power.cycle: 02 / THE SCHEDULE Low power is a schedule. I scheduled the firmware's power states. This teaching loop separates a device's work into three states. 01 Sleep Wait between work. 02 Measure Take a reading. 03 Transmit Send a report. ↶ Then back to Sleep. Explanatory teaching loop, not Mosslink's actual firmware. No timings or current values are shown. My working documents include state tables, timing diagrams and bench checklists: ways to describe the work to check.
beatText.middle.relationship: 03 / THE BENCH From a command to a check. Bring-up means checking a new board's basic operation. My fixture makes its response available to bench instruments. 01 Command 02 Board 03 Fixture 04 Observe Ada wrote the firmware and scheduled its power states. State tables and timing diagrams are part of her working documents; this is not a reproduction of that firmware. I wrote the firmware and built the fixture. A colleague designed the PCB and analogue front end. Command → board → fixture → observation. An explanatory relationship, not electrical wiring.
beatText.proof.boundaries: 04 / THE EVIDENCE Two numbers. Different evidence. INPUTS TO AN ESTIMATE MEASURED Sleep and transmit current on the bench. + ASSUMED The reporting interval. → 2 years Projected battery life A SEPARATE OBSERVATION A continuous run on the bench. → 72 hours The longest observed run Authored explanation of the supplied fictional notes, not the original spreadsheet or a measured trace. The run does not establish two years of operation. An estimate is not two years of observed operation.
beatText.close.evidence: 05 / THE SCOPE A connection. Not a leap. I connect firmware decisions to bench observations through power-state scheduling and the bring-up fixture, while keeping the evidence limits visible. Engineering samples assembled 40 Tested on the bench 6 Sent to customers 0 Six highlighted cells mark the bench-tested subset of forty. This illustrative count is not a pass/fail chart. One preliminary emissions check passed. Full qualification is unfinished. Read the source and limits ↘

Explanatory teaching loop, not Mosslink's actual firmware. No timings or current values are shown. My working documents include state tables, timing diagrams and bench checklists: ways to describe the work to check.
beatText.middle.relationship: 03 / THE BENCH From a command to a check. Bring-up means checking a new board's basic operation. My fixture makes its response available to bench instruments. 01 Command 02 Board 03 Fixture 04 Observe Ada wrote the firmware and scheduled its power states. State tables and timing diagrams are part of her working documents; this is not a reproduction of that firmware. I wrote the firmware and built the fixture. A colleague designed the PCB and analogue front end. Command → board → fixture → observation. An explanatory relationship, not electrical wiring.
beatText.proof.boundaries: 04 / THE EVIDENCE Two numbers. Different evidence. INPUTS TO AN ESTIMATE MEASURED Sleep and transmit current on the bench. + ASSUMED The reporting interval. → 2 years Projected battery life A SEPARATE OBSERVATION A continuous run on the bench. → 72 hours The longest observed run Authored explanation of the supplied fictional notes, not the original spreadsheet or a measured trace. The run does not establish two years of operation. An estimate is not two years of observed operation.
